The Lagos State Deputy Governor, Obafemi Hamzat, has called for stronger research commercialisation and university-industry partnerships to translate academic discoveries into practical solutions and economic opportunities. Hamzat said Nigerian universities and research institutions needed to bridge the gap between research findings and commercially viable innovations to enable tertiary education to contribute more effectively to national development. He spoke on Tuesday through the Commissioner for Tertiary Education, Tolani Sule, who represented him at the 38th convocation lecture of Yaba College of Technology, Lagos. The lecture was titled, “From Silos to Synergy: Reimagining the Nigerian Tertiary Education System for National Transformation.” Hamzat, who identified the disconnect between research and commercial application as one of the structural barriers limiting the potential of tertiary education, said research should not end with academic publications but should also produce solutions that improve lives. He said, “A research paper that identifies a solution to an agricultural problem should have a pathway towards practical application. “A laboratory discovery that can improve healthcare should have a route towards testing, development and deployment. “An engineering innovation that can reduce production costs should have access to the partnerships and resources necessary to reach the market.” Make PUNCH part of your everyday experience. He urged tertiary institutions to establish stronger relationships with businesses and other stakeholders to facilitate the practical application of research findings. Hamzat also called for increased research funding, more effective innovation hubs and university-based enterprises to support the development and commercialisation of locally generated knowledge. He said the value of research should not be measured solely by the number of academic publications but also by the problems addressed, new knowledge contributed and practical solutions developed. He, however, noted that fundamental research must be protected, stressing that not every worthwhile discovery would have immediate commercial value. “A robust knowledge economy requires both curiosity-driven scholarship and targeted, problem-solving research. Our responsibility is to build a system that supports both,” he said. The deputy governor also urged industries to see tertiary institutions as strategic partners in developing knowledge, technology and enterprise rather than merely suppliers of labour. He asked private-sector organisations to invest in research, support innovation, offer internships, participate in curriculum reviews, provide mentorship and commission research addressing industry challenges. Hamzat further advocated stronger collaboration among universities, polytechnics and colleges of education, saying their different mandates were complementary rather than competitive. He said institutions should undertake joint research projects, share specialised facilities and develop multidisciplinary innovation centres to strengthen the country’s research and innovation ecosystem. In his remarks, the Rector of YABATECH, Dr Ibraheem Abdul, said the institution was strengthening its research, innovation and industry partnerships to ensure its programmes addressed national development needs. He said, “The future of tertiary education must be anchored on stronger connections between institutions and industries, between research and practical application, and between knowledge acquisition and economic opportunity.” Abdul listed the National Skills Qualification Framework, proposed Solar-Powered Smart Campus Ecosystem, YABATECH Digital Technology Academy and YabaTech Skills Centre as initiatives designed to strengthen competency-based training, digital skills and graduate employability. He added, “The measure of our success will not simply be the number of graduates we produce, but the difference they make in industry, enterprise, communities and the wider society.” The rector also disclosed that the presidential approval for the conversion of YABATECH into the Federal University of Technology and Vocational Studies, Yaba, would provide an opportunity to strengthen applied research, technological innovation and industry partnerships. The Chairman of the College’s Governing Council, Prof. Funso Afolabi, called for measurable outcomes in research, innovation and industry partnerships, saying institutional progress should be assessed through verifiable results rather than policy declarations. He said, “We must establish measurable indicators for research output, graduate employment, staff development, industry partnerships, innovation and internally generated revenue. Institutional progress should be assessed against established baselines, annual targets and verifiable outcomes.” Afolabi also said the institution’s conversion into a university should translate into improved research capacity, academic excellence, technological innovation and global competitiveness, stressing that “a change in nomenclature alone does not constitute transformation.” Wale Akinselure Olawale Franklin Akinselure is a journalist at Punch Newspapers with 12 years of experience covering education, politics, health, environment, judiciary, metro, and community beats.
